newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Dec 10.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Dec 10.

text.p: New Zealanders are expected to find out on Tuesday who forms their new government. The NZ First caucus meets at 10 a.m. on Tuesday to choose between coalition offers settled in an intense day of political activity on Monday. The National caucus met for almost four hours on Monday to approve the party's coalition offer, with Prime Minister Jim Bolger emerging to say he had overwhelming support for the deal. Labour was negotiating with the Alliance till almost 10 p.m. to secure Alliance support for a possible Labour-NZ First coalition. Labour leader Helen Clark said discussions had been "very constructive". Tuesday's NZ
First caucus meeting is due to continue till a consensus or majority decision emerges, with an announcement of the result expected late Tuesday afternoon or Tuesday night. Page 1.

The Serious Fraud Office said on Monday it planned to lay criminal charges against importers of Japanese used cars in the next few months. It did not reveal how many importers would be targeted, but said tens of thousands of car buyers had been fleeced of million of dollars by dealers winding back odometers on Japanese imports. Page 1.

Sir Ronald Davison will be paid about $840,250 for his work as the Winebox inquiry commissioner from July last year till March next year, according to figures from the Internal Affairs Department. Page 1.

A cut-price airline begins flights across the Tasman from Auckland this weekend, just months after the collapse of budget-priced Kiwi International Airlines. Central Pacific Airlines will fly to Brisbane three times a week and Melbourne once a week. Its trans-tasman fares start from $465 return with a special fare of $445 for travellors over 60. Page 2.

The main operations of the government's state sector machine have slowed to a crawl since the election, while the public and their servants wait for NZ First to form a coalition government. However, State Services Commission chief Don Hunn said the contingency plans put in place appeared to have stood up the test of seven weeks of coalition negotiations. Page 2.

The high dollar is posing a risk to expectations for moderate economic growth in the next five years, according to forecasting group Institute of Economic Research. The dollar has risen as the Reserve Bank has battled to get underlying inflation below two percent by pushing short-term interest rates to some of the highest levels in the world. The group says widening the Reserve Bank's inflation target may be the key to getting a fall in the value of the dollar without significant economic cost. Page 13.

Continued reform was essential for New Zealand to reach its potential, former Fletcher Challenge and Business Roundtable chairman Sir Ron Trotter said on Monday. Trotter sketched a catalogue of changes outstanding at a World Bank conference on New Zealand's privatisation experience in Wellington, saying the ACC scheme was a "debt-ridden and divisive national disgrace", while the country wallowed in mediocrity in health and education. Page 13.

The agenda of a World Bank conference on privatisation held in Wellington on Monday was loaded in favour of privatisations, trade union speakers said. Council of Trade Unions economist Peter Harris told the 40 to 50 international delegates at the conference that the unions were not happy that there would be 24 speakers either advocating privatisation or examining it and only two against. Page 13.

ASB Bank managing director Ralph Norris said on Monday he expected the bank to report a net profit of just over $80 million in the year to June 1997, up from $71.8 million in the June 1996 year. Page 14.

It is understood that the policy compromise which drew the most heat in the National caucus was the deferring of the scheduled July 1 tax cuts. The length of the deferment could not be confirmed on Monday night but it is expected to be no more than 12 months.

International food and softdrink giant Pepsico is planning a $200 million joint float of its New Zealand KFC and Pizza Hut operations. It is expected that the float will take place in the first quarter of next year. Investment banker FR Partners is understood to be handling the issue, which will be marketed in New Zealand and the United States. It is unclear what stake, if any, Pepsico will retain in the listed vehicle. The move comes with Pepsico looking to franchise its major territories.

Financial markets are expecting an increase in spending by the new coalition government, but not to an extent which hurts investment assets, according to Spicers Financial Planners. Confidence that the outcome of the coalition negotiations will ultimately be market friendly has buoyed local markets, spokesman Aaron Hing said.

Competition from non-bank lenders had been given more credence than it deserved, but they were nevertheless acting to squeeze margins, ASB Bank managing director Ralph Norris said on Monday. "The new entrants to the market have not taken very much market share at all," he said.

After seven years in overseas ownership, Feltex Carpets is believed to be about to return to New Zealand ownership.
